claims.text: A live crawling louse is the strongest evidence of active infestation (Key Takeaways; #treatment p1; #diagnosis table; FAQ 1-2; #evidence last paragraph; alert box).
claims.quote: Finding a live nymph (baby louse) or adult louse on the scalp or hair is the best way to diagnose a head lice infestation.

claims.text: Nits can remain after successful treatment (Key Takeaways; #nits p1; FAQ 3).
claims.quote: Nits may stay in hair after treatment, but successful treatment will kill crawling lice.

claims.text: Nits can be mistaken for dandruff and other debris such as hair-product residue (Key Takeaways; #diagnosis p2; FAQ 2).
claims.quote: Nits are often confused with other particles found in hair such as dandruff, hair spray droplets, and dirt particles.

claims.text: Head lice are insects that live on the scalp and feed on blood (#diagnosis p1).
claims.quote: Head lice, or Pediculus humanus capitis, are parasitic insects that feed on human blood.

claims.text: A fine-toothed comb and examination behind the ears and near the nape help find lice and nits (#diagnosis p1; #combing p1).
claims.quote: A fine-toothed louse comb may help you find lice. ... You will often see nits on hair behind the ears and near the back of the neck.

claims.text: Nits more than one-quarter inch from the scalp are usually hatched or dead (#diagnosis p3).
claims.quote: Nits that are attached more than ¼ inch from the base of the hair shaft are almost always hatched or dead.

claims.text: Only distant nits without live nymphs or adults suggests an old infestation that may not need treatment (#diagnosis p3, p4; FAQ 3).
claims.quote: If you do not see nymphs or adults, and the only nits found are more than ¼ inch from the scalp, then the infestation is probably old and does not need treatment.

claims.text: Lice are small and can be hard to find in one quick look (#nits p2).
claims.quote: Because adult and nymph lice are very small, move quickly, and avoid light, they may be difficult to find.

claims.text: Light or early infestation may cause little itching (#nits p3).
claims.quote: People with head lice may not have symptoms, particularly with a first infestation or when an infestation is light.

claims.text: If the diagnosis is uncertain, ask a clinician (alert box; #treatment p1; #diagnosis p2; #care p3; home remedies p5).
claims.quote: If you are not sure if a person has head lice, see your healthcare provider.

claims.text: Misdiagnosis is common, so uncertain findings should be clarified before more treatment (#treatment p1; home remedies p5).
claims.quote: Misdiagnosis of head lice infestation is common.

claims.text: Scratching can cause scalp sores that may become infected (#treatment scope paragraph; #combing p5; #care p1).
claims.quote: Sores on the head caused by scratching, which can sometimes become infected with bacteria normally found on your skin

claims.text: Wash and dry items used in the two days before treatment; vacuum where the person sat or lay (#treatment p3; #contacts p3).
claims.quote: Machine wash and dry clothing, towels, bed linens, and other items that a person infested with lice wore or used during the two days before treatment.

claims.text: Hot-water target of 130 degrees Fahrenheit with high-heat drying; seal unwashable items for two weeks (#contacts p4).
claims.quote: Use the hot water (130°F) laundry cycle and the high heat drying cycle. If you can't wash or dry clean items, seal them in a plastic bag and store them for two weeks.

claims.text: Large amounts of time and money on whole-house decontamination are not necessary (#contacts p3).
claims.quote: However, spending much time and money on housecleaning activities is not necessary to avoid reinfestation by lice or nits that may have fallen off the head or crawled onto furniture or clothing.

claims.text: Do not spray the home; fumigant sprays or fogs are unnecessary and can be toxic (Key Takeaways; #treatment p3; #contacts p5; FAQ 11).
claims.quote: Do not use fumigant sprays or fogs; they are not necessary to control head lice and can be toxic if inhaled or absorbed through the skin.

claims.text: Lice spread mainly by direct hair contact, crawl rather than hop or fly, are not a hygiene problem, and pets do not spread them (#contacts p6).
claims.quote: Head lice mainly spread by direct contact with the hair of a person infested with lice. Head lice move by crawling; they cannot hop or fly.

claims.text: Head lice are not a sign of poor hygiene and animals do not spread them (#contacts p6).
claims.quote: Getting head lice is not related to cleanliness of you or your environment. ... Animals do not get or spread head lice.

references.notes: This page does not name permethrin or discuss resistance-gene prevalence. The permethrin non-ovicidal statement was re-pointed to ref 3 (CDC clinical care) and ref 9; the resistance-gene sentence was cut. Treatment-failure list items are joined with semicolons in the quote below (bulleted list on the page).

claims.text: Check household members and close contacts; treat infested people and those who share a bed with them at the same time (Key Takeaways; #treatment p3; #contacts p1-p2; FAQ 1, 11).
claims.quote: Check all household members and other close contacts for head lice. Treat all infested persons (household members and close contacts) and people they share a bed with at the same time.

claims.text: Treatment failure can reflect misdiagnosis, conditioner use, not following instructions, resistance or reinfestation; failure does not prove resistance (Key Takeaways; #treatment p1; #permethrin p5; #follow-up failure paragraphs; #care p5; FAQ 12).
claims.quote: Misdiagnosis; Recent application of combination shampoo/conditioner or conditioner to hair; Not following treatment instructions; Head lice resisting the medication; Reinfestation after successful treatment

claims.text: A few slow-moving lice 8 to 12 hours after treatment do not need reapplication (#treatment p4; #follow-up p2; FAQ 10).
claims.quote: If you notice a few lice still moving slowly 8 – 12 hours after treatment, you do not need to reapply the medicine. It takes time to kill all the lice.

claims.text: If lice are as active as before treatment, talk to a healthcare provider before retreating (alert box; citable summary; #treatment p4; #permethrin p4; #spinosad p6; #follow-up p2; FAQ 10).
claims.quote: If, 8 – 12 hours after treatment, you do not find any dead lice, or the lice seem as active as before treatment, the medicine may not be working. Talk to your healthcare provider before re-treating.

claims.text: A clinician may suggest a different medicine when treatment is not working (#follow-up p5; #spinosad p6).
claims.quote: Talk to your healthcare provider before re-treating. They may suggest a different medicine.

claims.text: Nit removal is not required with spinosad (#nits p4; #spinosad p3; #ivermectin p5 context; #combing p4; FAQ 8).
claims.quote: You do not need to remove nits when treating with spinosad topical suspension.

claims.text: Check hair and remove nits and lice every 2 to 3 days for 2 to 3 weeks after treatment (#follow-up p3).
claims.quote: After each treatment, check hair and remove nits and lice every 2 – 3 days for the next 2 – 3 weeks.

claims.text: Do not use conditioner before lice medicine (#combing p4; #follow-up failure paragraph).
claims.quote: Do not use a combination shampoo/conditioner, or conditioner, before using lice medicine.

claims.text: Some lice medications may cause itching or a mild burning sensation (#nits p1, p3; home remedies p5).
claims.quote: Some medications may cause itching or a mild burning sensation.

claims.text: Some medicines kill lice and eggs so retreatment is usually not needed; others do not kill eggs and need retreatment, so follow-up depends on the product (#follow-up p1; #nits p4).
claims.quote: Some medicines kill lice and eggs; retreatment is usually not required for these. Other medicines kill lice but are not effective at killing eggs and so retreatment is recommended.

claims.text: CDC has no scientific evidence that suffocating lice with mayonnaise, olive oil, butter, margarine or similar substances works (home remedies p3).
claims.quote: The CDC does not have scientific evidence that suffocating head lice with mayonnaise, olive oil, margarine, butter, or similar substances is an effective form of treatment.

claims.text: CDC lists over-the-counter and prescription medications as the treatment options (home remedies p1; FAQ 9).
claims.quote: You can treat lice with either over-the-counter or prescription medications.

claims.text: Treatment for pubic lice differs from head lice (#treatment scope paragraph).
claims.quote: Treatment for pubic lice is different than treatment for head lice. Ensure you're following the right steps based on the type of lice infestation.

claims.text: Laundering at 130 degrees Fahrenheit with high-heat drying, or sealing for two weeks, for items used in the prior two days (#contacts p3-p4).
claims.quote: Use hot water (130°F) and high heat drying. If you can’t wash or dry clean items, seal them in a plastic bag for two weeks.

claims.text: Do not use fumigant sprays or fogs; they can be toxic (Key Takeaways; #treatment p3; #contacts p5).
claims.quote: Do not use fumigant sprays or fogs. They can be toxic if inhaled or absorbed through the skin.

claims.text: Enough product is needed to cover the hair and scalp; longer hair may need more (#comparison p4).
claims.quote: If you have shoulder-length hair or longer, you might need a second bottle.

claims.text: Follow each product label from start to finish, including its retreatment instructions (hero caption context; #treatment p2; #follow-up p1; #care p5).
claims.quote: Follow all provided instructions when using lice medication. ... Follow your medication's instructions for retreatment.

claims.text: Consult a healthcare provider before treating young children; a shared household does not justify using an adult prescription for a child (#contacts p2).
claims.quote: Consult your healthcare provider before treating young children.

references.notes: This page lists only permethrin 1% lotion and does not mention permethrin 5% cream; the 5% cream statement was rewritten and re-pointed to ref 9. It does state that permethrin does not kill unhatched eggs, so the permethrin ovicidal claim now cites this page.

claims.text: Permethrin kills live lice but not unhatched eggs; CDC says another treatment may be needed on day nine (#permethrin p3-p4; FAQ 5; comparison table).
claims.quote: Permethrin kills live lice but not unhatched eggs. Permethrin can kill newly hatched lice for several days after treatment. You may need to treat again on day nine to kill any newly hatched lice before they can produce new eggs.

claims.text: Lice have some resistance to 1% permethrin but its prevalence is unknown (#permethrin p5).
claims.quote: Lice have developed some resistance to 1% permethrin, but prevalence of resistance is unknown.

claims.text: Ivermectin lotion kills lice and appears to prevent newly hatched nymphs from surviving although it does not kill eggs; effective as a single application on dry hair without nit combing (#ivermectin p2, p5; #nits p4).
claims.quote: It kills lice and, although it does not kill eggs, appears to prevent nymphs (newly hatched lice) from surviving. It is effective in most patients when given as a single application on dry hair without nit combing.

claims.text: Do not reuse ivermectin lotion without talking to a healthcare provider (Key Takeaways; #ivermectin p3; FAQ 6).
claims.quote: It should not be used for retreatment without talking to a healthcare provider.

claims.text: Oral ivermectin is not FDA-approved for lice (off-label) and is separate from the lotion (#ivermectin p6; #comparison p3).
claims.quote: Although not FDA-approved for the treatment of lice, ivermectin tablets given in a single oral dose of 200 micrograms/kg or 400 micrograms/kg repeated in 9-10 days are also effective against head lice.

claims.text: Malathion 0.5% is another option and is flammable; avoid smoking and electrical heat sources while hair is wet (#comparison p3; home remedies p4).
claims.quote: Malathion can irritate skin and is flammable. Do not smoke or use electrical heat sources, including hair dryers, curlers, and curling or flat irons, when applying malathion lotion and while the hair is wet.

claims.text: CDC also describes benzyl alcohol lotion (#comparison p3).
claims.quote: Benzyl alcohol is an aromatic alcohol. It kills lice but does not kill eggs.

claims.text: Spinosad kills live lice and unhatched eggs, so retreatment is usually unnecessary and nit combing is not required (#spinosad p2-p3; #follow-up p3; FAQ 7).
claims.quote: Since it kills live lice as well as unhatched eggs, retreatment is usually not needed. Nit combing is not required.

claims.text: Repeat spinosad only if live lice are seen seven days after the first treatment (#spinosad p2; FAQ 7).
claims.quote: Repeat treatment only if live (crawling) lice are seen seven days after the first treatment.

claims.text: Do not combine different lice medicines or use all three products; ask before combining (#treatment p2, p4; #nits p2; alert box).
claims.quote: Do not use different head lice drugs at the same time unless instructed to do so by your healthcare provider or pharmacist.

claims.text: Lice medicines are insecticides that can be dangerous if misused or overused; do not use extra amounts (home remedies p2, p5; #comparison p4; #spinosad p6).
claims.quote: Do not use extra amounts of any lice medication unless instructed to do so by your physician and pharmacist. The drugs used to treat lice are insecticides and can be dangerous if misused or overused.

claims.text: Consider an alternative medicine if crawling lice remain after a full course; a clinician may choose an alternative after an adequate course fails (#follow-up p5; #spinosad p6; #care p3; FAQ 12).
claims.quote: If crawling lice are still present after a full course of treatment and retreatment, consider an alternative medication.

claims.text: Do not keep repeating the same failed medicine; incorrect use or resistance can reduce effectiveness (alert box; #follow-up failure paragraph).
claims.quote: Do not treat a person infested with lice more than 2 – 3 times with the same medication if it isn't successful. Incorrect use of or resistance to medicine can reduce effectiveness.

claims.text: Over-the-counter and prescription products include permethrin 1% lotion, ivermectin 0.5% lotion and spinosad 0.9% suspension (#treatment p2).
claims.quote: Both over-the-counter and prescription medications are available to effectively treat head lice.

claims.text: Product ages and safety differ; a household member's prescription is not automatically suitable for someone else (#contacts p2).
claims.quote: Spinosad topical suspension is approved for the treatment of children six months of age and older.

claims.text: Permethrin is non-ovicidal and typically needs a repeat application (#permethrin p4).

claims.text: Permethrin 5% cream is first-line for scabies; permethrin 1% lotion or shampoo is first-line for head lice (#permethrin p6).
claims.quote: First-line pharmacologic treatment for pediculosis is permethrin 1% lotion or shampoo. ... First-line treatment for scabies is permethrin 5% cream.

claims.text: A dimethicone product sold under the Nix name has different directions from the permethrin rinse (#permethrin p2).
claims.quote: Noninsecticidal agents that rely on suffocation or exoskeleton dissolution include benzyl alcohol 5% lotion (Ulesfia), dimethicone solution (Nix Ultra, Lice MD), and isopropyl myristate solution

claims.text: An alternative agent after adequate courses fail (#follow-up p5).
claims.quote: After trials of two appropriately administered courses of permethrin, an alternative agent should be used.

claims.text: Wet combing is a repeated mechanical treatment done every three days until no lice are seen on four to five consecutive occasions (#combing p2).
claims.quote: Wet combing should be done every three days until no lice are detected on four to five consecutive occasions.

claims.text: Wet combing avoids chemicals but is time-consuming; cure rates vary and studies are not high quality (#combing p3; FAQ 9).
claims.quote: Wet combing alone does not have adverse effects and is often preferred by parents wanting to avoid a chemical treatment; however, it can be time-consuming.

claims.text: Cure rates for wet combing vary considerably and the studies are not high quality (#combing p3).
claims.quote: Cure rates vary considerably (47% to 75%), although studies are not high quality.

claims.text: Wet combing uses conditioner, which differs from medicine preparation (#combing p4).
claims.quote: moistening the hair with commercially available leave-in conditioner, combing with a wide-tooth comb until detangled, and then systematically combing the hair from root to tip with a lice comb

claims.text: Extensive environmental decontamination is not necessary; no sprays or chemical decontamination (Key Takeaways; #treatment p3; #contacts p3, p5; FAQ 11).
claims.quote: Sprays, carpet treatments, and other chemical environmental decontamination measures should not be used.

claims.text: Extensive environmental decontamination is not necessary (#treatment p3; #contacts p3).
claims.quote: Extensive environmental decontamination is not necessary after pediculosis is diagnosed.

claims.text: Lice cannot jump or fly; transmission requires close contact (#contacts p6).
claims.quote: Because lice cannot jump or fly, transmission requires close contact.

claims.text: Pubic lice should prompt an STI evaluation in adults; body lice are managed mainly by laundering (#treatment scope paragraph).
claims.quote: In adults, the presence of pubic lice should prompt an evaluation for sexually transmitted infections.

claims.text: Scratching can lead to excoriations and possible secondary cellulitis (#combing p5; #care p1).
claims.quote: Intense pruritus leads to scratching, with subsequent excoriations and possible secondary cellulitis.

claims.text: Itching is a delayed reaction; a person may itch little early on (#nits p3).
claims.quote: The pruritus associated with pediculosis is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, which may take four to six weeks to develop after the first exposure

claims.text: Lice are often overdiagnosed and self-treated without evaluation; irritation can be mistaken for more lice (home remedies p5; #care p5).
claims.quote: Lice in particular may be overdiagnosed by anxious patients and treated using over-the-counter medications without an office evaluation.

claims.text: Oral ivermectin is prescription-only and off-label for head lice (#ivermectin p6; #comparison p3).
claims.quote: Ivermectin, oral (Stromectol); prescription

claims.text: The 2019 review lists ivermectin 0.5% lotion as a prescription product (#evidence p4).
claims.quote: Ivermectin 0.5% lotion (Sklice); prescription

claims.text: Items in contact with the head in the two days before treatment should be washed (#contacts p3).
claims.quote: items that have come into direct contact with the head (e.g., pillowcases, hats, clothing) within the two days before treatment should be washed.

claims.text: Repeat check of what is found and clinical review distinguish other causes of itch (#care p3; #combing p5).
claims.quote: Determining the specific etiology of pruritus based on history and physical examination findings is important.
